section: Practice (written by us, not from a UPSC paper): Inference, assumptions and tone

en.stem:
When a machine takes over a task, the usual fear is that the worker who did the task has nothing left to do. Often what happens is different. A job is a bundle of tasks, and a machine rarely takes the whole bundle. A clerk whose machine now adds the figures spends more time explaining them to customers. The work changes before it disappears. This is no comfort to a worker whose skills lay mainly in the task that was taken over, and the change is hardest on those who have the least time or money to learn something new.

Passage 1. Which of the following is the most logical inference from the passage?
options: Machines always create more jobs than they remove
Counting the tasks a machine can do may overstate the number of jobs that will be lost
Clerks are no longer needed
Workers should refuse to use machines
en.why: A job is a bundle of tasks and a machine rarely takes the whole bundle, so tasks taken over are not the same as jobs lost. The first option is too strong, the third contradicts the clerk example, and the fourth is a recommendation the author does not make.

Passage 1. The statement that the change is hardest on those with the least time or money to learn something new assumes that:
options: Machines are expensive
All workers want to change jobs
Employers pay for training
Learning new skills takes time or money
en.why: If learning cost neither time nor money, lacking them would not make the change harder. Deny the fourth option and the statement falls. If the third were true, the statement would be weaker, so it cannot be the assumption.

Passage 1. The author's attitude to the effect of machines on work is best described as:
options: Balanced, noting both adjustment and hardship
Alarmed
Wholly reassuring
Indifferent to workers
en.why: The author corrects the usual fear and then says this is no comfort to some workers. Both sides are given weight.

en.stem:
A historian works from what has survived, and what survives is not a fair sample of the past. Kings had inscriptions cut in stone; farmers did not. Temples and courts kept records; households mostly did not. The result is that the surviving record speaks loudly about a few and softly about the many. A careful historian therefore asks two questions of every source: what does it say, and whose voice is missing from it? The second question cannot always be answered, but asking it prevents silence from being mistaken for absence.

Passage 2. Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Inscriptions are unreliable and should be ignored
Farmers did not matter in the past
A group that left few records need not have been unimportant in its own time
Historians can recover every missing voice
en.why: The passage warns against taking silence for absence. So few records do not show little importance. The fourth option contradicts the last sentence.

Temples and courts kept records; households mostly did not. The result is that the surviving record speaks loudly about a few and softly about the many. A careful historian therefore asks two questions of every source: what does it say, and whose voice is missing from it? The second question cannot always be answered, but asking it prevents silence from being mistaken for absence.

Passage 2. The passage assumes that:
options: Whether a record survives depends partly on who made it and on what material
All kings recorded the truth
Households kept no records at all
Stone inscriptions are the oldest records
en.why: The claim that what survives is not a fair sample needs survival to be uneven across makers and materials. The third option is too strong: the passage says mostly did not.

Passage 2. With which of the following would the author most likely agree?
options: History should be written only from royal records
A source should be read both for what it says and for what it leaves out
Nothing can be known about the past
Farmers' lives were the same in every period
en.why: This restates the two questions the careful historian asks. The third option goes far beyond the author's caution.

en.stem:
People follow a rule more readily when they believe that it is applied to everyone alike. A queue works because each person can see that others are also waiting. Once a few are seen to walk to the front without consequence, those still waiting begin to ask why they should wait. The rule has not changed, but the reason for following it has weakened. Institutions lose trust in the same way, less through a single large failure than through small exceptions that everyone can see.

Passage 3. Which of the following follows from the passage?
options: Rules should never have exceptions
Large failures do not harm institutions
People follow rules only out of fear of punishment
Visible and unpunished exceptions can weaken obedience even among those who gain nothing from breaking the rule
en.why: Those still waiting begin to ask why they should wait. Their willingness falls because of what they see. The second option turns less through into not at all.

en.stem:

Institutions lose trust in the same way, less through a single large failure than through small exceptions that everyone can see.

Passage 3. The argument rests on the assumption that:
options: Queues are always fair
Institutions never make large mistakes
People's willingness to follow a rule depends partly on whether they see others following it
Most people want to break rules
en.why: Deny the third option: if what others do made no difference, the queue example and the conclusion about trust would both fail.

Passage 3. Consider these statements: 1. A rule can lose force without being changed. 2. A single large failure is the main way in which institutions lose trust. Which of the statements can be inferred from the passage?
options: Both 1 and 2
1 only
2 only
Neither 1 nor 2
en.why: Statement 1: the rule has not changed, but the reason for following it has weakened. Statement 2 is the opposite of the last sentence.

en.stem:
Students often treat sleep as time taken away from study. The night before an examination, many stay awake to read once more. Yet learning is not finished when the book is closed. During sleep the brain goes over what was taken in during the day and fixes part of it in memory. A student who cuts sleep to add an hour of reading may gain a little from the hour and lose more from the missed rest. It is surely wiser to stop at a sensible hour and let the night do its share of the work.

Passage 4. The advice to stop at a sensible hour assumes that:
options: Students do not study enough
All students need the same amount of sleep
Reading at night is harmful to the eyes
What sleep adds to memory is worth more than what the last hour of reading adds
en.why: The advice follows only if the rest is worth more than the extra hour. Deny that and there is no reason to stop.

Passage 4. Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: An extra hour of reading on the night before an examination can leave a student worse prepared
Students should not study in the evening
Sleep matters more than study
Everything read during the day is fixed in memory during sleep
en.why: The student may gain a little and lose more. The fourth option turns part of it into everything. The third compares sleep and study in general, which the passage does not do.

Passage 4. The tone of the last sentence of the passage is:
options: Mocking
Doubtful
Advisory and confident
Neutral and descriptive
en.why: The sentence recommends a course, and the word surely shows confidence. It is not merely descriptive.

en.stem:
A market works well when buyers can judge what they are buying. For a bag of rice, a look and a feel are enough. For a medicine or an insurance policy they are not: the buyer cannot test the product and learns of a defect only when it is too late. In such markets a rule that sets a minimum standard does not work against the market. It supplies the confidence without which careful buyers would stay away and honest sellers would lose to careless ones. Whether a particular rule is well designed is a separate question.

Passage 5. Which of the following is the most logical inference from the passage?
options: Every market needs minimum standards
Where buyers cannot judge quality, a minimum standard can help the market itself to work
Rules always help honest sellers
Rice should not be regulated
en.why: The passage limits its claim to markets where the buyer cannot test the product. The first and third options drop that limit, and the fourth is a recommendation the passage does not make.

en.stem:

In such markets a rule that sets a minimum standard does not work against the market. It supplies the confidence without which careful buyers would stay away and honest sellers would lose to careless ones. Whether a particular rule is well designed is a separate question.

Passage 5. The claim that without confidence honest sellers would lose to careless ones assumes that:
options: Careless sellers break the law
Honest sellers are few
Buyers never return to the same seller
Buyers who cannot tell the good product from the bad tend to choose on price
en.why: The honest seller loses only if the buyer, unable to see quality, goes by something else such as price, where the careless seller can undercut. The third option is too strong to be needed.

Passage 5. What does the last sentence of the passage show about the author's position?
options: The author defends minimum standards in principle without defending every rule
The author opposes regulation
The author thinks most rules are badly designed
The author has no view
en.why: The author argues for standards in such markets and then sets aside, as a separate question, whether a particular rule is well made. That is a qualified position.
